sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.body: This plan maintains ongoing awareness of information security, vulnerabilities and threats to support risk decisions. It follows the NIST ISCM process: define, establish, implement, analyze and report, respond, and review and update.

sections.heading: 2. Scope
sections.body: The information systems, controls and environment in scope for continuous monitoring across the organisation.

sections.heading: 3. Define the Strategy
sections.body:
A monitoring strategy is defined and grounded in risk:
- Monitoring is driven by organisational risk tolerance and the controls that matter most.
- [FILL IN: state your risk tolerance and the priorities your monitoring supports.]

sections.heading: 4. Establish the Program
sections.body:
Metrics and frequencies are established:
- Security metrics are defined for the controls and outcomes being monitored.
- Monitoring and assessment frequencies are set from each item's volatility and risk.
- [FILL IN: list your key metrics and their monitoring frequency.]

sections.heading: 5. Implement the Program
sections.body:
Monitoring is carried out, using automation where possible:
- Data is collected from tools and assessments according to the defined frequencies.
- Automated collection is used where available to improve timeliness and coverage.

sections.heading: 6. Analyze and Report Findings
sections.body:
Data is analysed and reported to decision-makers:
- Collected data is analysed against the metrics and reported to the relevant stakeholders.
- Reporting supports risk-based decisions at the right level.

sections.heading: 7. Respond to Findings
sections.body:
Findings are acted on:
- Findings are mitigated, accepted, transferred or avoided as a risk decision.
- Actions are tracked to closure.

sections.heading: 8. Review and Update
sections.body:
The program is kept effective:
- The monitoring strategy and program are reviewed and updated as risk, systems and threats change.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.body: This policy protects the integrity of platform firmware and its critical data, and ensures the organisation can detect and recover from corruption. It follows the NIST firmware resiliency properties of Protection, Detection and Recovery.

sections.heading: 2. Scope
sections.body: Platform firmware on clients, servers and network devices, including system BIOS/UEFI, baseboard management controllers and the firmware of critical components.

sections.heading: 3. Protection
sections.body:
Firmware and its critical data are protected from unauthorised modification:
- Firmware updates are authenticated (cryptographically signed) before they are applied.
- Firmware update mechanisms are protected so only authorised updates succeed.
- Critical platform data is protected against unauthorised change.

sections.heading: 4. Detection
sections.body:
Corruption of firmware or critical data is detected:
- Platform integrity is measured and verified (for example at boot, using a root of trust).
- Unauthorised or unexpected firmware changes are detected and alerted.
- [FILL IN: name your platform integrity / attestation capability.]

sections.heading: 5. Recovery
sections.body:
Firmware can be restored to a known-good state:
- A protected recovery mechanism can restore firmware after detected corruption.
- Recovery images are authenticated before use.
- Recovery is tested so it works when needed.

sections.heading: 6. Lifecycle and Inventory
sections.body:
Firmware is managed across the device lifecycle:
- Devices are sourced and accepted with firmware integrity verified (see hardware supply-chain controls).
- Firmware versions are inventoried and kept current within vendor support.
- End-of-support devices are retired or compensated for.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.body: This policy governs how cryptographic keys are generated, protected, used and retired so that the cryptography the organisation relies on remains trustworthy. It follows the NIST key-management lifecycle.

sections.heading: 2. Scope
sections.body: All cryptographic keys used to protect organisational information, in applications, infrastructure and third-party services.

sections.heading: 3. Approved Cryptography
sections.body:
Only approved, validated cryptography is used:
- Use cryptographic algorithms and key sizes that are currently approved by NIST.
- Prefer FIPS-validated cryptographic modules (see the cryptographic module inventory).
- [FILL IN: list your approved algorithms and minimum key sizes.]

sections.heading: 4. Key Lifecycle
sections.body:
Keys are managed across the pre-operational, operational, post-operational and destroyed phases:
- Generation: keys are generated using approved methods and strong random sources.
- Distribution and storage: private and secret keys are protected at all times, ideally in an HSM or key vault.
- Use: keys are used only for their intended purpose and within their cryptoperiod.
- Rotation: keys are rotated at the end of their cryptoperiod or on compromise.
- Revocation and destruction: compromised or retired keys are revoked and securely destroyed.
- Archival: keys needed to access archived data are retained and protected.

sections.heading: 5. Cryptoperiods
sections.body:
Each key has a defined cryptoperiod (the time a key is authorised for use), set from its type, usage and risk.
[FILL IN: set cryptoperiods for each key type you use.]

sections.heading: 6. Protection and Separation of Duties
sections.body:
Key-management duties and access are controlled:
- Access to keys is restricted on least privilege; sensitive operations require more than one person.
- Keys are never stored in source code, configuration files or alongside the data they protect.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.body: This policy ensures that information is removed from media before the media is reused, transferred or disposed of, so that data cannot be recovered. It is based on the NIST media sanitization decision of Clear, Purge or Destroy.

sections.heading: 2. Scope
sections.body: All storage media owned or controlled by the organisation, including computers, servers, mobile devices, removable media, printers and storage in cloud and on-premises systems.

sections.heading: 3. Sanitization Decision
sections.body:
The sanitization method is chosen from the security categorization of the information and whether the media will leave organisational control:
- Clear: apply logical techniques to sanitize data in all user-addressable locations, protecting against simple, non-invasive recovery.
- Purge: apply physical or logical techniques that make recovery infeasible using state-of-the-art laboratory techniques.
- Destroy: physically destroy the media so it cannot be reused and data cannot be recovered.
- Higher-confidentiality data, or media leaving organisational control, requires Purge or Destroy.

sections.heading: 4. Method by Media Type
sections.body:
The technique is matched to the media type using recognised methods:
- Flash and solid-state media: use the device's verified secure-erase or cryptographic erase; destroy where required.
- Magnetic hard drives: overwrite or degauss to Purge; shred or disintegrate to Destroy.
- Mobile devices: use a full factory reset with encryption (cryptographic erase) per the manufacturer.
- Paper and printed output: cross-cut shred.
- [FILL IN: list the media types you hold and the chosen method for each.]

sections.heading: 5. Verification
sections.body:
Sanitization is verified before media is released:
- A representative verification is performed after sanitization to confirm data was removed.
- Equipment and tools used for sanitization are tested and kept current.

sections.heading: 6. Documentation
sections.body: Each sanitization action is recorded on a Certificate of Sanitization (below) and retained as evidence.
